    58	openclaw security audit
    59	openclaw security audit --deep
    60	openclaw health
    61	```
    62	
    63	Resolve critical findings first. Accept warnings only when intentional and
    64	documented for the deployment. See [Security audit checks](/gateway/security/audit-checks)
    65	for what each `checkId` means and its fix key.
    66	
    67	For remote CLI validation, pass credentials explicitly:
    68	
    69	```bash
    70	openclaw gateway probe --url ws://127.0.0.1:18789 --token "$OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_TOKEN"
    71	```
    72	
    73	Do not assume local config credentials apply to an explicit remote URL.
    74	
    75	## Minimum safe baseline
    76	
    77	Use this shape as the starting point for exposed deployments:
    78	
    79	```json5
    80	{
    81	  gateway: {
    82	    bind: "loopback",
    83	    auth: {
    84	      mode: "token",
    85	      token: "replace-with-a-long-random-token",
    86	    },
    87	  },
    88	  session: {
    89	    dmScope: "per-channel-peer",
    90	  },
    91	  agents: {
    92	    defaults: {
    93	      sandbox: { mode: "non-main" },
    94	    },
    95	  },
    96	  tools: {
    97	    profile: "messaging",
    98	    exec: { security: "deny", ask: "always" },
    99	    elevated: { enabled: false },
   100	  },
   101	}
   102	```
   103	
   104	Widen one control at a time: add a specific channel allowlist before enabling
   105	write-capable tools, or enable a reverse proxy before accepting remote Control
   106	UI traffic.
   107	
   108	`tools.exec.security: "deny"` blocks all exec calls, including benign
   109	diagnostics. If diagnostics or low-risk commands are required, relax this only
   110	after choosing the specific senders, agents, commands, and approval mode that
   111	match your threat model.
   112	
   113	## DM and group exposure
   114	
   115	Messaging channels are untrusted input surfaces. Before allowing DMs or
   116	groups:
   117	
   118	- Prefer `dmPolicy: "pairing"` or a strict `allowFrom` list over `dmPolicy: "open"`.
   119	- Do not combine `"*"` allowlists with broad tool access.
   120	- Require mentions in groups unless the room is tightly controlled.
   121	- Set `session.dmScope: "per-channel-peer"` (or `"per-account-channel-peer"` for
   122	  multi-account channels) when multiple people can DM the bot, so DM sessions
   123	  don't share context.
   124	- Route shared channels to agents with minimal tools and no personal
   125	  credentials.
   126	
   127	Pairing approves the sender to trigger the bot. It does not make that sender a
   128	separate host security boundary.
   129	
   130	## Reverse proxy checks
   131	
   132	For identity-aware proxies:
   133	
   134	- The proxy must authenticate users before forwarding to the Gateway.
   135	- Firewall or network policy must block direct access to the Gateway port.
   136	- `gateway.trustedProxies` must list only the proxy source IPs.
   137	- The proxy must strip or overwrite client-supplied identity and forwarding
   138	  headers.
   139	- Set `gateway.auth.trustedProxy.allowUsers` when the proxy serves more than
   140	  one audience.
   141	- Use `gateway.auth.trustedProxy.allowLoopback` only for a same-host proxy
   142	  where local processes are trusted and the proxy owns the identity headers.
   143	
   144	Run `openclaw security audit --deep` after proxy changes. Trusted-proxy
   145	findings are high-signal because the proxy becomes the authentication
   146	boundary.
   147	
   148	## Tool and sandbox review
   149	
   150	Before exposing an agent to remote senders:
   151	
   152	- Confirm which sessions run on host versus sandbox.
   153	- Deny or require approval for host exec.
   154	- Keep elevated tools disabled unless a specific, trusted sender needs them.
   155	- Avoid browser, canvas, node, cron, gateway, and session-spawn tools for open
   156	  or semi-open messaging surfaces.
   157	- Keep bind mounts narrow; avoid credential, home, Docker socket, and system
   158	  paths.
   159	- Use separate gateways, OS users, or hosts for materially different trust
   160	  boundaries.
   161	
   162	If remote users are not fully trusted, isolation must come from separate
   163	deployments, not only from prompts or session labels.
   164	
   165	## Post-change validation
   166	
   167	After each exposure change:
   168	
   169	1. Re-run `openclaw security audit --deep`.
   170	2. Confirm a successful authorized connection succeeds.
   171	3. Confirm an unauthorized sender or browser session is denied.
   172	4. Confirm log tails, console output, and exports redact secrets; keep raw log files private.
   173	5. Confirm DM/group routing reaches only the intended agent.
   174	6. Confirm high-impact tools ask for approval or are denied.
   175	7. Document the accepted residual warnings.
   176	
   177	Do not proceed to the next exposure change until the current one is
   178	understood.
   179	
   180	## Rollback plan
   181	
   182	If the Gateway may be overexposed:
   183	
   184	```json5
   185	{
   186	  gateway: {
   187	    bind: "loopback",
   188	  },
   189	  channels: {
   190	    whatsapp: { dmPolicy: "disabled" },
   191	    telegram: { dmPolicy: "disabled" },
   192	    discord: { dmPolicy: "disabled" },
   193	    slack: { dmPolicy: "disabled" },
   194	  },
   195	  tools: {
   196	    exec: { security: "deny", ask: "always" },
   197	    elevated: { enabled: false },
   198	  },
   199	}
   200	```
   201	
   202	Then:
   203	
   204	1. Stop public forwarding, Tailscale Funnel, or reverse proxy routes.
   205	2. Rotate Gateway tokens/passwords and affected integration credentials.
   206	3. Remove `"*"` and unexpected senders from allowlists.
   207	4. Review recent audit logs, run history, tool calls, and config changes.
   208	5. Re-run `openclaw security audit --deep`.
   209	6. Re-enable access with the narrowest pattern that satisfies the workflow.
   210	
   211	## Review checklist
   212	
   213	- Gateway remains loopback-only unless there is a documented reason.
   214	- Non-loopback access has auth, firewalling, and no public direct route.
   215	- Trusted-proxy deployments have strict proxy IPs and header controls.
   216	- DMs use pairing or allowlists, not open access by default.
   217	- Groups require mentions or explicit allowlists.
   218	- Shared channels do not reach personal credentials.
   219	- Non-main sessions run in sandbox mode.
   220	- Host exec and elevated tools are denied or approval-gated.
   221	- Log tails, console output, and exports redact secrets; raw log files stay private.
   222	- Critical audit findings are resolved.
   223	- Rollback steps are tested and documented.

     8	
     9	## Hardened baseline in 60 seconds
    10	
    11	```json5
    12	{
    13	  gateway: {
    14	    mode: "local",
    15	    bind: "loopback",
    16	    auth: { mode: "token", token: "replace-with-long-random-token" },
    17	  },
    18	  session: {
    19	    dmScope: "per-channel-peer",
    20	  },
    21	  tools: {
    22	    profile: "messaging",
    23	    deny: ["group:automation", "group:runtime", "group:fs", "sessions_spawn", "sessions_send"],
    24	    fs: { workspaceOnly: true },
    25	    exec: { security: "deny", ask: "always" },
    26	    elevated: { enabled: false },
    27	    sessions: { visibility: "agent" },
    28	    agentToAgent: { enabled: false },
    29	  },
    30	  channels: {
    31	    whatsapp: { dmPolicy: "pairing", groups: { "*": { requireMention: true } } },
    32	  },
    33	}
    34	```
    35	
    36	Keeps the Gateway local-only, isolates DMs, limits session tools to the agent's own sessions, turns off ordinary cross-agent access, and disables control-plane/runtime tools by default. Re-enable tools selectively per trusted agent from there.
    37	
    38	Built-in baseline for chat-driven agent turns: non-owner senders cannot use the `cron` or `gateway` tools regardless of config.
    39	
    40	### Requester-scoped controls and prompt context
    41	
    42	`tools.toolsBySender`, sender ownership, and owner-only tool inventories are evaluated against the current turn's originating requester. They do not authenticate or sanitize other content in that model prompt, including quoted text, prior shared-room history, forwarded content, fetched content, attachments, tool results, or other prompt inputs. Content from another person can therefore influence an owner-triggered turn when it is included in that turn's context.
    43	
    44	Treat these controls as defense in depth that reduces direct capability for a requester, not as hostile multi-user isolation. Use `contextVisibility` to filter supported channel-supplied context, restrict tools and sandbox the agent, and use separate gateways and ideally separate OS users or hosts when participants are mutually adversarial.
    45	
    46	## Secure baseline (copy/paste)
    47	
    48	```json5
    49	{
    50	  gateway: {
    51	    mode: "local",
    52	    bind: "loopback",
    53	    port: 18789,
    54	    auth: { mode: "token", token: "your-long-random-token" },
    55	  },
    56	  channels: {
    57	    whatsapp: {
    58	      dmPolicy: "pairing",
    59	      groups: { "*": { requireMention: true } },
    60	    },
    61	  },
    62	}
    63	```
    64	
    65	Keeps the Gateway private, requires DM pairing, and gates group replies behind a mention. Groups are fully supported - sender identity is threaded through to the agent, and per-group settings let one room run different defaults than another - so the goal here is scoping the agent's attention, not avoiding groups. For safer tool execution too, add a sandbox + deny dangerous tools for any non-owner agent (see "Per-agent access profiles" above).
    66	
    67	### Separate numbers (WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram)
    68	
    69	For phone-number-based channels, consider running the assistant on a separate number from your personal one, so personal conversations stay private and the bot number handles automation with its own boundaries.

     9	---
    10	
    11	## Incident response
    12	
    13	### Contain
    14	
    15	1. Stop it: stop the macOS app (if it supervises the Gateway) or terminate your `openclaw gateway` process.
    16	2. Close exposure: set `gateway.bind: "loopback"` (or disable Tailscale Funnel/Serve) until you understand what happened.
    17	3. Freeze access: switch risky DMs/groups to `dmPolicy: "disabled"` / require mentions, and remove any `"*"` allow-all entries.
    18	
    19	### Rotate (assume compromise if secrets leaked)
    20	
    21	1. Rotate Gateway auth (`gateway.auth.token` / `gateway.auth.password`). Rotation hot-applies only when the effective auth mode stays the same; set `gateway.auth.mode` explicitly for SecretRefs. Restart for an auth-mode change or updated process environment credentials such as `OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PASSWORD`.
    22	2. Rotate remote client secrets (`gateway.remote.token` / `.password`) on any machine that can call the Gateway.
    23	3. Rotate provider/API credentials (WhatsApp creds, Slack/Discord tokens, model/API keys in SQLite auth stores, and encrypted secrets payload values when used).
    24	
    25	### Audit
    26	
    27	1. Check Gateway logs with `openclaw logs` (or `openclaw --profile <profile> logs` for a named profile). Default files are under the selected state directory's `logs/` directory, unless `logging.file` overrides it; see [log locations](/logging#where-logs-live).
    28	2. Review the relevant transcript(s): `~/.openclaw/agents/<agentId>/sessions/*.jsonl`.
    29	3. Review recent config changes that could have widened access: `gateway.bind`, `gateway.auth`, DM/group policies, `tools.elevated`, plugin changes.
    30	4. Re-run `openclaw security audit --deep` and confirm critical findings are resolved.
    31	
    32	### Collect for a report
    33	
    34	- Timestamp, gateway host OS + OpenClaw version.
    35	- The session transcript(s) + a short log tail (after redacting).
    36	- What the attacker sent and what the agent did.
    37	- Whether the Gateway was exposed beyond loopback (LAN/Tailscale Funnel/Serve).

     1	---
     2	summary: "How OpenClaw triages, responds to, and follows up on security incidents"
     3	title: "Incident response"
     4	read_when:
     5	  - Responding to a security report or suspected security incident
     6	  - Preparing a coordinated disclosure or patched security release
     7	  - Reviewing post-incident follow-up expectations
     8	---
     9	
    10	## 1. Detection and triage
    11	
    12	Security signals come from:
    13	
    14	- GitHub Security Advisories (GHSA) and private vulnerability reports.
    15	- Public GitHub issues/discussions when reports are not sensitive.
    16	- Automated signals: Dependabot, CodeQL, npm advisories, secret scanning.
    17	
    18	Initial triage:
    19	
    20	1. Confirm affected component, version, and trust boundary impact.
    21	2. Classify as a security issue vs. hardening/no-action, using `SECURITY.md`'s scope and out-of-scope rules.
    22	3. An incident owner responds accordingly.
    23	
    24	## 2. Severity
    25	
    26	| Severity | Definition                                                                                                                                                                            |
    27	| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
    28	| Critical | Package/release/repository compromise, active exploitation, or unauthenticated trust-boundary bypass with high-impact control or data exposure.                                       |
    29	| High     | Verified trust-boundary bypass requiring limited preconditions (for example, authenticated but unauthorized high-impact action), or exposure of OpenClaw-owned sensitive credentials. |
    30	| Medium   | Significant security weakness with practical impact but constrained exploitability or substantial prerequisites.                                                                      |
    31	| Low      | Defense-in-depth findings, narrowly scoped denial-of-service, or hardening/parity gaps without a demonstrated trust-boundary bypass.                                                  |
    32	
    33	## 3. Response
    34	
    35	1. Acknowledge receipt to the reporter (privately when sensitive).
    36	2. Reproduce on supported releases and latest `main`, then implement and validate a patch with regression coverage.
    37	3. Critical/high: prepare patched release(s) as fast as practical.
    38	4. Medium/low: patch in the normal release flow and document mitigation guidance.
    39	
    40	## 4. Communication and disclosure
    41	
    42	Communicate through GitHub Security Advisories in the affected repository, release notes/changelog entries for fixed versions, and direct reporter follow-up on status and resolution.
    43	
    44	Critical/high incidents get coordinated disclosure, with CVE issuance when appropriate. Low-risk hardening findings may be documented in release notes or advisories without a CVE, depending on impact and user exposure.
    45	
    46	## 5. Recovery and follow-up
    47	
    48	After shipping the fix:
    49	
    50	1. Verify remediations in CI and release artifacts.
    51	2. Run a short post-incident review: timeline, root cause, detection gap, prevention plan.
    52	3. Add follow-up hardening/tests/docs tasks and track them to completion.
    53	
    54	## Related
    55	
    56	- [Security policy](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/SECURITY.md) — report scope and trust model.
    57	- [Threat model](/security/THREAT-MODEL-ATLAS)
    58	- [Contributing to the threat model](/security/CONTRIBUTING-THREAT-MODEL) — how to add a threat to the living threat model; not the path for reporting a live vulnerability.
    59	- [Formal verification](/security/formal-verification) — machine-checked models of authorization, session isolation, and tool gating.
    60	- [Operator incident response](/gateway/security/operator-incident-response) — contain, rotate, audit, and collect evidence after a suspected compromise of your own Gateway.

     1	---
     2	summary: "What `openclaw security audit` inspects and the order to fix its findings in"
     3	read_when:
     4	  - You changed config and want to know whether you drifted from safe defaults
     5	  - You are about to expose a network surface
     6	  - You have audit findings and need a triage order
     7	title: "Running the security audit"
     8	sidebarTitle: "Running the audit"
     9	---
    10	
    11	## `openclaw security audit`
    12	
    13	Run this after any config change or before exposing network surfaces:
    14	
    15	```bash
    16	openclaw security audit
    17	openclaw security audit --deep    # attempts a live Gateway check
    18	openclaw security audit --fix     # apply safe remediations
    19	openclaw security audit --json
    20	```
    21	
    22	`--fix` is intentionally narrow: it flips open group policies to allowlists, tightens state/config/include-file permissions (`600` files, `700` dirs), and on Windows uses ACL resets instead of POSIX `chmod`.
    23	
    24	### What the audit checks (high level)
    25	
    26	- **Inbound access** - DM/group policies, allowlists: can strangers trigger the bot?
    27	- **Cross-agent session access** - two or more agents with default Gateway-wide session visibility and unrestricted agent-to-agent access: `info` for one operator's personas, `warn` when sandboxing, agent-level tool restrictions, or shared-user ingress suggest different trust levels. Fully sandboxed rosters under the default spawn-tree clamp produce no finding; setting `agents.defaults.sandbox.sessionToolsVisibility` to `"all"` disables that exemption.
    28	- **Potential tool damage** - elevated tools + open rooms: could prompt injection become shell/file/network actions?
    29	- **Exec filesystem drift** - mutating filesystem tools denied while `exec`/`process` stay available without sandbox constraints.
    30	- **Exec approval drift** - `security="full"`, `autoAllowSkills`, interpreter allowlists without `strictInlineEval`. `security="full"` alone is a broad posture warning, not proof of a bug - it is the chosen default for trusted-operator setups; tighten it only when your threat model needs approval or allowlist guardrails.
    31	- **Network exposure** - Gateway bind/auth, Tailscale Serve/Funnel, weak/short auth tokens and passwords.
    32	- **Browser control exposure** - remote nodes, relay ports, remote CDP endpoints.
    33	- **Local disk hygiene** - permissions, symlinks, config includes, synced-folder paths.
    34	- **Plugins** - loading without an explicit allowlist.
    35	- **Policy drift** - sandbox Docker settings configured but sandbox mode off; `gateway.nodes.commands.deny` entries that look effective but only match exact command IDs (for example `system.run`), not shell text inside the payload; dangerous `gateway.nodes.commands.allow` entries; global `tools.profile="minimal"` overridden per agent; plugin-owned tools reachable under a permissive policy.
    36	- **Runtime expectation drift** - assuming implicit exec still means `sandbox` when `tools.exec.host` now defaults to `auto`, or setting `tools.exec.host="sandbox"` while sandbox mode is off.
    37	
    38	Each finding has a structured `checkId` (for example `gateway.bind_no_auth`, `tools.exec.security_full_configured`). Prefixes: `fs.*` (permissions), `gateway.*` (bind/auth/Tailscale/Control UI/trusted-proxy), `hooks.*`/`browser.*`/`sandbox.*`/`tools.exec.*` (per-surface hardening), `plugins.*`/`skills.*` (supply chain), `security.exposure.*` (access policy x potential tool damage), `security.trust_model.*` (shared-context and cross-agent defaults). Full catalog with severity and auto-fix support: [Security audit checks](/gateway/security/audit-checks). See also [Formal Verification](/security/formal-verification).
    39	
    40	### Priority order when triaging findings
    41	
    42	1. Anything "open" + tools enabled: lock down DMs/groups first (pairing/allowlists), then tighten tool policy/sandboxing.
    43	2. Public network exposure (LAN bind, Funnel, missing auth): fix immediately.
    44	3. Browser control remote exposure: treat like operator access (tailnet-only, pair nodes deliberately, no public exposure).
    45	4. Permissions: state/config/credentials/auth must not be group/world-readable.
    46	5. Plugins: load only what you explicitly trust.
############ web/control-ui/security-model.md ############
     1	---
     2	summary: "Content security policy, public transcript boundaries, authenticated media routes, and approval links"
     3	read_when:
     4	  - Reviewing Control UI browser security
     5	  - Exposing public session links through a login proxy
     6	  - Debugging a blocked avatar or assistant media request
     7	  - Forwarding an approval link
     8	title: "Security model"
     9	sidebarTitle: "Security model"
    10	---
    11	
    12	How the Control UI restricts the browser and authenticates its own routes.
    13	
    14	## Content security policy
    15	
    16	The Control UI allows **same-origin** assets, `data:` URLs, locally generated `blob:` URLs, and remote HTTPS images. Remote HTTP images are blocked. Protocol-relative image URLs follow the document's scheme.
    17	
    18	In practice:
    19	
    20	- Avatars and images served under relative paths (for example `/avatars/<id>`) still render, including authenticated avatar routes the UI fetches and converts into local `blob:` URLs.
    21	- Inline `data:image/...` URLs still render.
    22	- Local `blob:` URLs created by the Control UI still render. Text attachment previews can read those local bytes before the attachment is sent.
    23	- HTTPS transcript images render in Chat image galleries and Activity previews. The browser contacts the image host directly, disclosing its network address; thumbnails, the expanded image viewer, and neighboring-image preloads send no page referrer.
    24	- Markdown attachment and Skill Workshop previews keep remote images as click-to-open links. Plugin README and agent-file previews automatically load HTTPS images and contact their hosts directly from the browser.
    25	- Verified GitHub profile photos render through the authenticated Gateway avatar route, with uploaded OpenClaw photos taking precedence. Session-only readers can request images by exact profile ID without access to the private People directory. Device-token authority is revalidated after asynchronous image preparation and before the response is disclosed. The Gateway fetches only identity-owner-built GitHub URLs, with bounded time and bytes and no redirects. Publication account choices render from `avatars.githubusercontent.com` or, for GitHub Enterprise accounts, the account's GitHub host. The Gateway builds these URLs from verified account IDs; avatar helpers continue to reject arbitrary remote avatar URLs.
    26	- GitHub link preview avatars are fetched by the Gateway from GitHub's fixed avatar host and returned as bounded `data:` URLs; the operator browser never contacts the remote avatar host.
    27	- Link favicons are on by default. The authenticated Control UI requests them through the Gateway; the browser never contacts link destinations directly. The link-favicon route requests each public hostname's HTTPS `/favicon.ico`, with strict DNS-pinned SSRF checks on the original URL and every redirect plus bounded time, bytes, concurrency, and image validation. Private, internal, and IP-literal destinations are rejected. This discloses linked hostnames and the Gateway's network address to those sites. Ordinary external-link hover previews also fetch the public page’s title, bounded description, declared favicon, and Open Graph or Twitter social image through the authenticated Gateway. These anonymous requests never use browser cookies or site c…
    28	- Animated PNG (APNG) icons are accepted as PNG images. Workspace icons and managed channel avatars retain their animation; remote plugin, catalog, and link icons use a resized PNG preview.
    29	- Remote avatar URLs emitted by channel metadata are stripped at the Control UI's avatar helpers and replaced with the built-in logo/badge, so a compromised or malicious channel cannot force arbitrary remote image fetches from an operator browser.
    30	
    31	Page metadata reads stop at the end of the HTML head or after 64 KiB, whichever
    32	comes first; metadata beyond that limit is omitted. The Gateway streams the head
    33	without building a page DOM. Anonymous previews use a bounded cache per requesting
    34	principal and runtime config revision for one hour when available, or five minutes
    35	when unavailable; URL fragments share the same entry. Repeated links share pending
    36	requests, and a page that declares the same social image and favicon downloads it
    37	once. The 15-second preview deadline includes queue wait, fetching, and image work.
    38	Disabling automatic favicons or retiring the request's authority suppresses cached
    39	previews too.
    40	
    41	The browser-side CSP restriction itself is always on and not configurable.
    42	
    43	## Connection permissions
    44	
    45	The Control UI uses the granted scopes returned by the Gateway handshake.
    46	Session readers can open shared chats without polling operator-only dashboards,
    47	scheduled tasks, voice catalogs, or provider authentication status. Restricted
    48	surfaces are hidden or show an access message. A dashboard `FORBIDDEN` response
    49	stops automatic retries; reconnecting replaces the connection's granted scopes.
    50	The Gateway continues to authorize every request and subscription.
    51	
    52	## Public transcript boundary
    53	
    54	Public threads use the same `/chat/...` URL as the authenticated Control UI.
    55	Anonymous readers receive a separate, read-only document, never an operator
    56	connection. **Log in** goes through a protected same-origin handoff and returns
    57	to that thread with the person's existing permissions. Identity headers on the
    58	anonymous thread path do not authorize private access. Private and missing
    59	threads have the same anonymous unavailable response.
    60	
    61	In token/password deployments, the reader can recognize a browser-held session
    62	token or paired-device credential scoped to the current Gateway address and base
    63	path. After the protected probe returns `401`, that presence is only a navigation
    64	hint to open the app shell; the reader never sends the credential or authorizes
    65	session data. The app's existing WebSocket and bootstrap checks still apply.
    66	A `204` probe continues into the app, while `403` keeps the public reader even
    67	when local credentials exist. Trusted-proxy and external-login handoffs retain
    68	their existing authentication and permission checks.

    15

    11	
    12	OpenClaw uses `pnpm-lock.yaml` as its committed product dependency review boundary. It records the resolved dependency graph used by source checkouts and CI, so transitive changes remain visible in code review.
    13	
    14	OpenClaw does not commit npm-format locks for product packages or publish them in package tarballs. [npm 12 removed shrinkwrap support](https://github.com/npm/cli/releases/tag/v12.0.0), including the `npm shrinkwrap` command and loading `npm-shrinkwrap.json` from package roots or dependency tarballs.

    19	
    20	## Check dependency advisories
    21	
    22	Ordinary pull-request, push, and scheduled CI do not run the production dependency audit. The `security-fast` job runs it only for `workflow_dispatch` IDs beginning with `full-release-validation-` or `release-native-android-`. These release checks and the optional production audit pre-commit hook print audit findings and turn every audit failure into a warning with exit code 0, including unavailable or invalid advisory data. A passing result is limited to that source and graph; it does not establish that dependencies are unaffected by all known vulnerabilities.
    25	
    26	`pnpm deps:vuln:gate`, used by release dependency evidence, audits the target's product pnpm lock plus each release-tool lock whose package is present in that target. It checks npm advisory data and adds published security advisories from verified public GitHub repositories. Repository mappings come from the manifests for exact locked npm package versions, not a package's latest manifest.     27

    31

    33	
    34	Release artifacts and the GitHub Actions step summary show npm coverage as `checked`, upstream coverage as `checked` or `partial`, mapped package-version counts, checked repository counts, coverage issues, and upstream-only findings.     41

    43	
    44	Published OpenClaw plugin packages bundle their runtime dependency files in the tarball by default. Those bytes ship with the plugin and work the same way regardless of whether the operator uses npm, pnpm, or Bun.
    45	
    46	Native-heavy plugins opt out of runtime dependency bundling because their dependency trees contain platform-specific or large native artifacts. Those plugins resolve dependencies at install time from exact-pinned direct dependencies. The root `openclaw` package also resolves dependencies at install time and does not bundle its full dependency tree.
    47	
    48	When preparing a package that carries bundled dependencies, OpenClaw also declares its hoisted optional platform packages as root `optionalDependencies`, using the validated npm dependency graph.     49

   127	
   128	Gateway HTTP bearer auth is effectively all-or-nothing operator access. Credentials that can call `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses`, plugin routes such as `/api/v1/admin/rpc`, or `/api/channels/*` are full-access operator secrets for that gateway: shared-secret bearer auth restores the full default operator scopes (`operator.admin`, `operator.approvals`, `operator.pairing`, `operator.read`, `operator.talk.secrets`, `operator.write`) and owner semantics for agent turns, and narrower `x-openclaw-scopes` values do not reduce that shared-secret path. Per-request scope semantics only apply when the request comes from an identity-bearing mode (trusted proxy auth) or an explicitly no-auth private ingress; in those modes, omitting `x-openclaw-scopes`…
   129	
   130	Tokenless Serve auth assumes the gateway host itself is trusted - it is not protection against hostile same-host processes. If untrusted local code may run on the gateway host, disable `allowTailscale` and require explicit shared-secret auth (`token` or `password`).
   131	
   132	An externally managed Tailscale Serve or Funnel route may forward these headers to the ordinary listener only through an explicitly configured `gateway.trustedProxies` source with a valid non-loopback forwarded client address. OpenClaw treats that request as generic proxy ingress: the configured gateway auth applies, `allowTailscale` grants nothing, and no WhoIs lookup runs. Gateway-protected routes reject external Funnel ingress when auth mode is `none`; aggregate health, readiness, and startup checks keep their bounded unauthenticated responses. See [Tailscale](/gateway/tailscale#externally-managed-serve-and-funnel), [Health and readiness](/gateway/health), and [Trusted Proxy Auth](/gateway/trusted-proxy-auth).
   133	
   134	See [Tailscale](/gateway/tailscale) and [Web overview](/web).
   135	
   136	### Reverse proxy configuration
   137	
   138	Set `gateway.trustedProxies` for proper forwarded-client IP handling behind nginx/Caddy/Traefik/etc. When the Gateway detects proxy headers from an address **not** in `trustedProxies`, it will not treat the connection as local; if gateway auth is disabled, that connection is rejected. This prevents proxied connections from appearing to come from localhost and receiving automatic trust.
   139	
   140	With token or password auth, an unconfigured same-host loopback proxy is
   141	rejected on Gateway-authenticated routes because OpenClaw cannot attribute its
   142	forwarded client headers. HTTP requests receive `403` with
   143	`proxy_attribution_required`; WebSocket auth fails with guidance to configure
   144	`gateway.trustedProxies`. Plugin-authenticated webhook routes retain their own
   145	signature or credential checks and ignore untrusted forwarded claims.
   146	Configure `trustedProxies` narrowly and make the proxy overwrite or safely
   147	rebuild forwarded headers; see [Rate
   148	limiting](/gateway/security/rate-limiting#unconfigured-same-host-reverse-proxies).
   149	
   150	`trustedProxies` also feeds `gateway.auth.mode: "trusted-proxy"`, which is stricter: it rejects loopback-source proxies by default. Same-host loopback reverse proxies can use `trustedProxies` for local-client detection and forwarded-IP handling, but can only satisfy `trusted-proxy` auth mode when `gateway.auth.trustedProxy.allowLoopback = true`; otherwise use token/password auth.
   151	
   152	```yaml
   153	gateway:
   154	  trustedProxies:
   155	    - "10.0.0.1" # reverse proxy IP
   156	  allowRealIpFallback: false # default false; only enable if your proxy cannot provide X-Forwarded-For
   157	  auth:
   158	    mode: password
   159	    password: ${OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PASSWORD}
   160	```
   161	
   162	When `trustedProxies` is set, the Gateway uses `X-Forwarded-For` to determine client IP; `X-Real-IP` is ignored unless `gateway.allowRealIpFallback: true` is explicitly set. Check that your proxy **overwrites** `X-Forwarded-For`/`X-Real-IP` rather than appending to them:
   163	
   164	```nginx
   165	# good
   166	proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr;
   167	proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
   168	
   169	# bad: preserves/appends untrusted client-supplied values
   170	proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
   171	```
   172	
   173	Trusted proxy headers do not make node device pairing automatically trusted - `gateway.nodes.pairing.autoApproveCidrs` is a separate, disabled-by-default operator policy, and loopback-source trusted-proxy header paths stay excluded from node auto-approval even when loopback trusted-proxy auth is enabled (because local callers can forge those headers).
   174	
   175	### Plugin remote Control UI ingress
   176	
   177	A trusted plugin such as [MCP Relay](/plugins/mcp-relay) can expose the
   178	[remote Control UI ingress](/plugins/sdk-gateway-ingress). Each grant is bound to
   179	the shared owner on a token or password Gateway without `gateway.roles`, or to a
   180	verified person on a Cloudflare Access trusted-proxy Gateway with roles. The
   181	plugin must authenticate the browser as its locally approved grant holder before
   182	forwarding any request or socket. Core treats the live handle like a trusted
   183	proxy: a browser with a signed device identity connects as an operator, with
   184	scopes limited to the grant's ceiling intersected with the principal's current
   185	authority. No reusable device token is issued. Shared Gateway secrets, bootstrap
   186	credentials, device-less connections, non-operator roles, and scopes above the
   187	ceiling are refused.
   188	
   189	The browser appears in **Devices** and `openclaw devices list` as a paired-device
   190	row kept for visibility and key checks. It holds no bearer credential that works
   191	on the Gateway's direct listener; every reconnect is admitted by the live grant.
   192	Revoke the plugin grant to end delegated access. Revocation closes the ingress
   193	path and its retained work without deleting the paired-device row.
   194	
   195	### HSTS and origin notes
   196	
   197	- OpenClaw's gateway is local/loopback first. If you terminate TLS at a reverse proxy, set HSTS there.
   198	- If the gateway itself terminates HTTPS, `gateway.http.securityHeaders.strictTransportSecurity` emits the HSTS header from OpenClaw responses.
   199	- Non-loopback Control UI deployments need configured browser origins: omit `gateway.controlUi.allowedOrigins` to use `gateway.publicOrigin`, or set an explicit list. An explicit list replaces the default; `allowedOrigins: ["*"]` allows every browser origin and should be avoided outside tightly controlled local testing.
   200	- Failed authentication from loopback is never locked out, so a local CLI cannot be denied before its credentials are checked. Wrong credentials are still tracked and progressively delayed (bounded delay, one shared timer per key); successful authentication resets only the matching credential-class history. This raises the cost of repeated guessing from one loopback source; it is not a defense against an attacker who can already open many parallel loopback connections, because credentials are compared before the failure response is delayed. Loopback reachability is a trust boundary in its own right - see [Node pairing](/gateway/pairing#silent-local-pairing).
   201	- Browser-origin auth failures on loopback are still rate-limited even with the general loopback exemption enabled, but the lockout key is scoped per normalized `Origin` value instead of one shared localhost bucket.
   202	- `gateway.controlUi.dangerouslyAllowHostHeaderOriginFallback=true` enables Host-header origin fallback mode; treat it as a dangerous operator-selected policy.
   203	- Treat DNS rebinding and proxy-host header behavior as deployment hardening concerns; keep `trustedProxies` tight and avoid exposing the gateway directly to the public internet.
   204	- Detailed deployment guidance: [Trusted Proxy Auth](/gateway/trusted-proxy-auth#tls-termination-and-hsts).
   205	
   206	### Control UI over HTTP
   207	
   208	The Control UI generates device identity with pure-JS Ed25519, so pairing works on any origin, including plain HTTP.
   209	
   210	- Token/password auth does not replace browser device identity: HTTP browsers still pair with a signed device key, which never crosses the wire. Prefer HTTPS (for example, Tailscale Serve) — plaintext transport still exposes the page and the shared secret to on-path attackers.
   211	- `gateway.controlUi.dangerouslyDisableDeviceAuth`: retired break-glass input, now fully inert. Control UI browsers pair through the normal device flow; `openclaw doctor --fix` removes the legacy key.
   212	- Separately, successful `gateway.auth.mode: "trusted-proxy"` authentication can admit **operator** Control UI sessions without device identity when the browser cannot supply one. Browsers that can mint an identity (any origin, including plain HTTP) follow the normal pairing flow instead — automatic with `deviceAutoApprove`, otherwise a one-time approval. This does not extend to node-role Control UI sessions.
   213	
   214	### Insecure/dangerous flags
   215	
   216	`openclaw security audit` raises `config.insecure_or_dangerous_flags` for each enabled known insecure/dangerous debug switch (one finding per flag). Keep these unset in production. If audit suppressions are configured, `security.audit.suppressions.active` stays in the active output even when matching findings move to `suppressedFindings`.
   217	
   218	<AccordionGroup>
   219	  <Accordion title="Flags tracked by the audit today">
   220	    - `gateway.controlUi.dangerouslyAllowHostHeaderOriginFallback=true`
   221	    - `security.audit.suppressions configured (<count>)`
   222	    - `hooks.gmail.allowUnsafeExternalContent=true`
   223	    - `hooks.mappings[<index>].allowUnsafeExternalContent=true`
   224	    - `tools.exec.applyPatch.workspaceOnly=false`
   225	    - `plugins.entries.acpx.config.permissionMode=approve-all`
   226	
   227	  </Accordion>
   228	
   229	  <Accordion title="All dangerous*/dangerously* keys in the config schema">
   230	    Control UI and browser:
   231	    - `gateway.controlUi.dangerouslyAllowHostHeaderOriginFallback`
   232	    - `gateway.controlUi.dangerouslyDisableDeviceAuth` (retired, inert)
   233	    - `browser.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork`
   234	
   235	    Channel name-matching (bundled and plugin channels; also per `accounts.<accountId>` where applicable):
   236	    - `channels.discord.dangerouslyAllowNameMatching`
   237	    - `channels.googlechat.dangerouslyAllowNameMatching`
   238	    - `channels.msteams.dangerouslyAllowNameMatching`
   239	    - `channels.slack.dangerouslyAllowNameMatching`
   240	    - `channels.irc.dangerouslyAllowNameMatching` (plugin channel)
############ cloudflare-access.md (1-90) ############
     1	---
     2	summary: "Publish a loopback Gateway through a Cloudflare Tunnel and authenticate every client with Cloudflare Access"
     3	read_when:
     4	  - You want a public HTTPS Gateway URL without opening a port
     5	  - You want Cloudflare Access (SSO) to authenticate the Control UI
     6	  - Your CLI, TUI, or nodes get HTTP 302 from a Cloudflare-fronted Gateway
     7	title: "Cloudflare Tunnel and Access"
     8	---
     9	
    10	Run the Gateway on loopback, publish it through a Cloudflare Tunnel, and let Cloudflare
    11	Access authenticate every request before it reaches OpenClaw. The Gateway keeps
    12	`gateway.bind: "loopback"`, so no port is exposed and no inbound firewall rule is
    13	needed; `cloudflared` dials out from the host.
    14	
    15	This is one supported remote-access topology alongside [Tailscale](/gateway/tailscale)
    16	and an [SSH tunnel](/gateway/remote). Choose it when you want a
    17	stable public HTTPS URL and identity-provider SSO in front of the Control UI.
    18	
    19	## Before you begin
    20	
    21	- A Cloudflare account with the zone for your hostname, and Cloudflare Zero Trust enabled.
    22	- `cloudflared` installed on the Gateway host, and on any machine that will use the CLI.
    23	- A running Gateway on `127.0.0.1:18789` with `gateway.bind: "loopback"`.
    24	- Familiarity with [trusted-proxy auth](/gateway/trusted-proxy-auth), which this topology uses.
    25	
    26	## How the pieces fit
    27	
    28	```text
    29	browser / CLI / node  ->  Cloudflare Access (identity)  ->  Tunnel  ->  127.0.0.1:18789
    30	```
    31	
    32	Access authenticates the request and injects identity headers. The Gateway does not
    33	re-authenticate the person or verify the Access JWT signature; it checks the trusted
    34	proxy source and configured header presence, then trusts the user header. Because
    35	`allowLoopback` also lets other local processes present those headers, keep the Gateway
    36	port private to the host and run only trusted workloads there.
    37	
    38	## Step 1: Route the tunnel to loopback
    39	
    40	Add an ingress rule mapping your hostname to the Gateway port, then run `cloudflared`
    41	as a service on the Gateway host:
    42	
    43	```yaml
    44	tunnel: <tunnel-id>
    45	credentials-file: /root/.cloudflared/<tunnel-id>.json
    46	ingress:
    47	  - hostname: gateway.example
    48	    service: http://localhost:18789
    49	  - service: http_status:404
    50	```
    51	
    52	See Cloudflare's own documentation for creating the tunnel and DNS record.
    53	
    54	## Step 2: Protect the hostname with Access
    55	
    56	Create an Access application for `gateway.example` with a policy that allows your
    57	users. Note the two headers Access adds to authenticated requests, because the Gateway
    58	consumes them in the next step:
    59	
    60	- `cf-access-authenticated-user-email` — the authenticated identity.
    61	- `cf-access-jwt-assertion` — Access's signed assertion. OpenClaw checks only that this
    62	  header is present and non-blank; it does not verify the JWT signature.
    63	
    64	### Email-code sign-in
    65	
    66	Cloudflare Access one-time PIN sign-in resolves a person through the existing
    67	verified-email profile. OpenClaw requires a successful Access identity response
    68	with the `onetimepin` provider and an email matching the authenticated user header.
    69	It does not infer GitHub credit from this identity. Access policies and OpenClaw
    70	role and access checks still apply; keep the Access policy limited to intended users.
    71	
    72	### OIDC sign-in and existing people
    73	
    74	For OIDC sign-in, configure an Access policy that admits the intended users through
    75	that identity provider. For example, use a signed role claim maintained by the
    76	provider. A GitHub organization policy applies to the GitHub identity provider;
    77	it does not grant access through a separate OIDC provider.
    78	
    79	OpenClaw verifies the OIDC identity through Cloudflare Access's identity endpoint
    80	and requires its email to match the authenticated user header. It then resolves
    81	that email through the existing person profile. Using the same email retains the
    82	person's profile and role; a different email requires an existing linked alias to
    83	resolve to that person. GitHub sign-in continues to verify the immutable GitHub
    84	account ID. Failed identity verification does not fall back to email matching.
    85	
    86	Successful identity lookups are reused for the same signed assertion, matching
    87	principal, and OIDC configuration for at most five minutes, never beyond the
    88	assertion's expiration. Concurrent matching requests share the lookup. Failures
    89	are not cached. Proxy admission and current profile roles are still checked on
    90	each request; this cache does not grant access or retain a role assignment.

    91	
    92	Keep the identity provider responsible for verifying email ownership. Creating an
    93	OpenClaw person profile does not grant access through Cloudflare Access.
    94	
    95	### Verified GitHub credit through OIDC
    96	
    97	An OIDC provider can supply a verified GitHub account without changing the sign-in
    98	email or the account used to publish pull requests. This is optional and disabled
    99	until you explicitly trust one Access issuer, identity-provider ID, and claim name:
   100	
   101	```json5
   102	{
   103	  gateway: {
   104	    auth: {
   105	      mode: "trusted-proxy",
   106	      trustedProxy: {
   107	        userHeader: "cf-access-authenticated-user-email",
   108	        requiredHeaders: ["cf-access-jwt-assertion"],
   109	        cloudflareAccessOidc: {
   110	          issuer: "https://example.cloudflareaccess.com",
   111	          providerId: "your-access-identity-provider-id",
   112	          githubAccountIdClaim: "https://openclaw.ai/github-account-id",
   113	        },
   114	      },
   115	    },
   116	  },
   117	}
   118	```
   119	
   120	The issuer is the Access team origin without a trailing slash. `providerId` is
   121	the selected integration's ID from Access, not its name or an OIDC user subject.
   122	The provider must verify ownership of the GitHub account and bind it to the
   123	verified sign-in email. Its ID token must contain a positive
   124	decimal-string account ID with no leading zeros, such as `"12345"`, within JavaScript's safe-integer
   125	range. Configure Access to forward that exact [custom OIDC claim](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/integrations/identity-providers/generic-oidc/#custom-oidc-claims).
   126	OpenClaw reads it from `oidc_fields` in the authenticated
   127	`/cdn-cgi/access/get-identity` response, or from `custom` when `oidc_fields` is
   128	absent, then verifies the numeric account through GitHub to obtain its current
   129	public login. A present `oidc_fields` container takes precedence: OpenClaw does
   130	not retry `custom` if the preferred container lacks the claim or its value is
   131	invalid. The identity-provider **Test** preview uses `oidc_fields`; inspect the
   132	authenticated identity endpoint after a fresh sign-in to verify the response
   133	OpenClaw consumes.
   134	
   135	A missing or malformed optional claim, or an unselected issuer/provider, keeps
   136	ordinary email-only resolution. Malformed claims are never sent to GitHub or
   137	used to create an association or public credit. If the optional GitHub account lookup fails, OpenClaw resolves the
   138	authenticated email through the normal profile and access-policy checks. An
   139	existing authorized profile or valid email invitation can still sign in. A
   140	GitHub-only access requirement is not satisfied by an email fallback.
   141	
   142	Lookup failure does not create a GitHub identity or public credit. An existing
   143	verified matching association and saved co-author preference remain intact;
   144	a later successful lookup can complete or refresh the link. This behavior
   145	applies to both `oidc_fields` and `custom`. Invalid Access authentication,
   146	mismatched principals, conflicting profile bindings for valid account claims,
   147	and expired or revoked access still fail their normal checks.
   148	
   149	Existing email profiles retain
   150	their identity, role, and saved co-author preference. A conflicting GitHub account
   151	does not automatically merge profiles or move the email; an administrator must
   152	resolve it through the existing `users.linkEmail` operation. This also applies
   153	to a first-time email claiming an account that already belongs to another
   154	profile: link that email explicitly before it can inherit the profile's role.
   155	Explicitly linked secondary accounts retain the profile's primary account for public credit.
   156	See [Gateway profiles and GitHub credit](/concepts/user-model#gateway-profile-and-github-credit).

   158	## Step 3: Trust those headers in the Gateway

   161	is required here: `cloudflared` connects from `127.0.0.1`, and trusted-proxy auth

   165	{
   166	  gateway: {
   167	    bind: "loopback",
   168	    publicOrigin: "https://gateway.example",
   169	    trustedProxies: ["127.0.0.1", "::1"],
   170	    auth: {
############ trusted-proxy-auth.md (1-110) ############
     1	---
     2	summary: "Delegate gateway authentication to a trusted reverse proxy (Pomerium, Caddy, nginx + OAuth)"
     3	title: "Trusted proxy auth"
     4	sidebarTitle: "Trusted proxy auth"
     5	read_when:
     6	  - Running OpenClaw behind an identity-aware proxy
     7	  - Setting up Pomerium, Caddy, or nginx with OAuth in front of OpenClaw
     8	  - Fixing WebSocket 1008 unauthorized errors with reverse proxy setups
     9	  - Deciding where to set HSTS and other HTTP hardening headers
    10	---
    11	
    12	<Warning>
    13	**Security-sensitive feature.** This mode delegates authentication entirely to your reverse proxy. Misconfiguration can expose your Gateway to unauthorized access. Read this page carefully before enabling.
    14	</Warning>
    15	
    16	## When to use
    17	
    18	- You run OpenClaw behind an **identity-aware proxy** (Pomerium, Caddy + OAuth, nginx + oauth2-proxy, Traefik + forward auth).
    19	- Your proxy handles all authentication and passes user identity via headers.
    20	- You're in a Kubernetes or container environment where the proxy is the only path to the Gateway.
    21	- You're hitting WebSocket `1008 unauthorized` errors because browsers can't pass tokens in WS payloads.
    22	
    23	## When NOT to use
    24	
    25	- Your proxy doesn't authenticate users (just a TLS terminator or load balancer).
    26	- There's any path to the Gateway that bypasses the proxy (firewall holes, internal network access).
    27	- You're unsure whether your proxy correctly strips/overwrites forwarded headers.
    28	- You only need personal single-user access (consider Tailscale Serve + loopback instead).
    29	
    30	## How it works
    31	
    32	<Steps>
    33	  <Step title="Proxy authenticates the user">
    34	    Your reverse proxy authenticates users (OAuth, OIDC, SAML, etc.).
    35	  </Step>
    36	  <Step title="Proxy adds an identity header">
    37	    Proxy adds a header with the authenticated user identity (e.g., `x-forwarded-user: nick@example.com`).
    38	  </Step>
    39	  <Step title="Gateway verifies trusted source">
    40	    OpenClaw checks that the request came from a **trusted proxy IP** (`gateway.trustedProxies`). Loopback sources require explicit `allowLoopback` consent; other Gateway-local interface addresses are rejected.
    41	  </Step>
    42	  <Step title="Gateway extracts identity">
    43	    OpenClaw reads the required headers, then the user identity from the configured header.
    44	  </Step>
    45	  <Step title="Authorize">
    46	    If everything checks out, and the user passes `allowUsers` (when set), the request is authorized.
    47	  </Step>
    48	</Steps>
    49	
    50	## Configuration
    51	
    52	```json5
    53	{
    54	  gateway: {
    55	    // Trusted-proxy auth expects the proxy's source IP to be non-loopback by default
    56	    bind: "lan",
    57	
    58	    // CRITICAL: Only add your proxy's IP(s) here
    59	    trustedProxies: ["10.0.0.1", "172.17.0.1"],
    60	
    61	    auth: {
    62	      mode: "trusted-proxy",
    63	      identityScopes: {
    64	        "admin@company.org": ["operator.admin"],
    65	      },
    66	      trustedProxy: {
    67	        // Header containing authenticated user identity (required)
    68	        userHeader: "x-forwarded-user",
    69	
    70	        // Optional: headers that MUST be present (proxy verification)
    71	        requiredHeaders: ["x-forwarded-proto", "x-forwarded-host"],
    72	
    73	        // Optional: restrict to specific users (empty = allow all)
    74	        allowUsers: ["nick@example.com", "admin@company.org"],
    75	
    76	        // Optional: allow a same-host loopback proxy after explicit opt-in
    77	        allowLoopback: false,
    78	
    79	        // Optional: let authenticated proxy users enroll UI devices and upgrade scopes
    80	        deviceAutoApprove: {
    81	          enabled: false,
    82	          scopes: ["operator.read", "operator.write", "operator.approvals", "operator.questions"],
    83	        },
    84	      },
    85	    },
    86	  },
    87	}
    88	```
    89	
    90	<Warning>
    91	**Runtime rules, in order of evaluation**
    92	
    93	1. Proxy-shaped traffic is attributed before Gateway auth. The request's source IP must match `gateway.trustedProxies` (CIDR-aware), and its client-address headers must resolve to a non-loopback client. Otherwise Gateway-authenticated routes reject it with `proxy_attribution_required` before identity headers are accepted. Plugin-authenticated webhook routes may still handle the request, but they ignore the untrusted forwarded address and use the socket source for their own limits.
    94	2. The proxy must overwrite `X-Forwarded-For` with a safe chain. If `gateway.allowRealIpFallback = true`, an overwritten `X-Real-IP` is also accepted when `X-Forwarded-For` is absent. Do not enable that fallback unless the proxy removes client-supplied `X-Real-IP`.
    95	3. Loopback-source requests (`127.0.0.1`, `::1`) are rejected unless `gateway.auth.trustedProxy.allowLoopback = true` and the loopback address is also in `trustedProxies` (`trusted_proxy_loopback_source`). This check runs before header checks, so a loopback source fails this way even if required headers are also missing.
    96	4. Non-loopback sources that match one of the Gateway host's own local network interface addresses are rejected as a spoofing guard (`trusted_proxy_local_interface_source`). If interface discovery itself fails, the request is rejected too (`trusted_proxy_local_interface_check_failed`).
    97	5. `requiredHeaders` and `userHeader` must be present and non-blank.
    98	6. `allowUsers`, if non-empty, must include the extracted user.
    99	
   100	**Forwarded-header evidence overrides loopback locality for local-direct fallback.** If a request arrives on loopback but carries a `Forwarded`, any `X-Forwarded-*`, or `X-Real-IP` header, that evidence disqualifies it from local-direct password fallback and device-identity gating, even though it still fails trusted-proxy auth as loopback.
   101	
   102	The same restriction always applies to Tailscale identity headers. While OpenClaw ID
   103	is on (`gateway.openclawId.enabled`), it also applies to Cloudflare Access identity
   104	headers, `Remote-User`, `X-Remote-User`, and the configured `userHeader` or
   105	`requiredHeaders`: an identity-only request without a usable forwarded client
   106	address is rejected, not treated as the local operator. This protects OpenClaw
   107	ID's local-only linking; see [access coexistence](/gateway/remote#openclaw-id-alongside-existing-access).
   108	With OpenClaw ID off, those headers do not change loopback locality.
   109	
   110	`allowLoopback` trusts local processes on the Gateway host to the same degree as the reverse proxy. Enable it only when the Gateway is still firewalled from direct remote access and the local proxy strips or overwrites client-supplied identity headers.

70:### Workspace `.env` files
72:OpenClaw loads workspace-local `.env` files for agents and tools, but never lets them silently override gateway runtime controls:
74:- Provider credential environment variables are blocked from untrusted workspace `.env` files - for example `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `GOOGLE_API_KEY`, `XAI_API_KEY`, `MISTRAL_API_KEY`, `GROQ_API_KEY`, `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`, `PERPLEXITY_API_KEY`, `BRAVE_API_KEY`, `TAVILY_API_KEY`, `EXA_API_KEY`, `FIRECRAWL_API_KEY`, and provider auth keys declared by installed trusted plugins. Put provider credentials in the Gateway process environment, `~/.openclaw/.env` (`$OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR/.env`), the config `env` block, or an optional login-shell import instead.
75:- Any key starting with `OPENCLAW_` is blocked from untrusted workspace `.env` files, reserving the whole runtime namespace so a future `OPENCLAW_*` control is blocked by default rather than silently inheritable from checked-in or attacker-supplied `.env` content.
76:- Channel and provider endpoint-routing settings are also blocked from workspace `.env` overrides (for example `MATRIX_HOMESERVER`, `MATTERMOST_URL`, `IRC_HOST`, `SYNOLOGY_CHAT_INCOMING_URL`, `AZURE_SPEECH_ENDPOINT`, and other keys ending in `_ENDPOINT`), so a cloned workspace cannot redirect bundled connector traffic through local endpoint config. These must come from the gateway process environment, global runtime dotenv, explicit config, or `env.shellEnv`.
77:- Executable search-path roots are blocked from workspace `.env` files (for example `PATH`, `PNPM_HOME`, `NPM_CONFIG_PREFIX`, `MISE_DATA_DIR`, and `XDG_BIN_HOME`). For package-manager roots supplied by the trusted environment, the CLI PATH bootstrap rejects relative or workspace-contained candidates before adding them to child-process `PATH`. Inherited `PATH` entries remain operator-controlled, including relative and workspace-local entries.
78:- Trusted process/OS environment variables, global runtime dotenv, config `env`, and enabled login-shell import still apply - this only constrains workspace `.env` file loading.
80:Workspace `.env` files frequently live next to agent code, get committed by accident, or get written by tools; blocking provider credentials prevents a cloned workspace from substituting attacker-controlled provider accounts.

88:Gateway logs may include tool summaries, errors, and URLs; session transcripts can include pasted secrets, file contents, command output, and links.
90:- File logs store raw records with owner-only (`0600`) permissions. Log tails (`logs.tail`), console output, diagnostics/support bundles, and remote/OTel export mask sensitive values independently. Direct file reads are raw; protect them like the agent/state databases. Session transcripts, tool arguments, tool results, and `.env` reads preserve their original text, including credentials.

     1	# Security Policy
     2	
     3	If you believe you've found a security issue in OpenClaw, report it privately first.
     4	
     5	This policy does two things: it gives researchers a clear disclosure path, and it spells out the trust model maintainers use when triaging reports. OpenClaw is local-first agent infrastructure for trusted operators; it is not designed as a shared multi-tenant boundary between adversarial users on one gateway.
     6	
     7	The fastest useful reports show a current, reproducible boundary bypass with demonstrated impact. Scanner output, prompt-injection-only chains, or reports that rely on hostile users sharing one trusted gateway are usually not security vulnerabilities under this model.

    10	
    11	## Shared Agents
    12	
    13	Anyone who can operate an agent can make it do anything that agent can do. Session ownership, visibility, and presence are usability features, not security boundaries. Turn attribution is best-effort because steering can merge input into an active turn. Use separate agents or separate gateway/host trust boundaries when operators need real isolation.
    14	
    15	## Report a Security Issue
    16	
    17	Report vulnerabilities directly to the repository where the issue lives:
    18	
    19	- **Core CLI and gateway** — [openclaw/openclaw](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw)

    23	- **ClawHub** — [openclaw/clawhub](https://github.com/openclaw/clawhub)
    24	
    25	For issues that don't fit a specific repo, or if you're unsure, email **[security@openclaw.ai](mailto:security@openclaw.ai)** and we'll route it.
    26	
    27	For OpenClaw core issues, submit through a private [GitHub Security Advisory](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/security/advisories/new). Do not open a public issue or PR that discloses an unpatched vulnerability, exploit path, secret, or security-sensitive proof of concept.
    28	
    29	Maintainers may close, hide, delete, or otherwise take down public issues and PRs that disclose vulnerabilities or active security issues. We will redirect those reports through the private disclosure process so the issue can be triaged and fixed without giving attackers a public playbook.
    30	
    31	For full reporting instructions see our [Trust page](https://trust.openclaw.ai).
    32	For maintainer response workflow, see the [incident response plan](docs/security/incident-response.md).
    33	
    34	OpenClaw does not currently run a paid bug bounty program. Please still disclose responsibly so we can fix real issues quickly. The best way to help the project right now is to send high-signal reports and, when practical, focused PRs.
    35	
    36	### What We Need
    37	
    38	Make the report easy to reproduce and easy to route:
    39	
    40	- What you found and why you believe it is security-relevant.
    41	- The affected component, version, and commit SHA when possible.
    42	- Reproduction steps or a proof of concept against latest `main` or the latest released version.
    43	- The actual impact, including which OpenClaw trust boundary is crossed.
    44	- Any remediation advice or focused patch you can provide.
    45	
    46	Reports without reproduction steps, demonstrated impact, and remediation advice are deprioritized. We receive a high volume of AI-generated scanner findings, so we prioritize vetted reports from researchers who can show how the issue crosses an OpenClaw security boundary.
    47	
    48	### What Usually Is Not a Security Bug
    49	
    50	These patterns are usually not vulnerabilities by themselves:
    51	
    52	- Prompt injection without a policy, auth, approval, sandbox, or tool-boundary bypass.
    53	- A trusted operator using an intentional local feature, such as local shell access or browser/script execution.
    54	- A report whose only primitive is changing the process or child-process environment before running OpenClaw or an executable OpenClaw invokes.
    55	- A malicious plugin after a trusted operator installs or enables it.
    56	- Multiple adversarial users sharing one Gateway host/config and expecting per-user isolation.
    57	- Scanner-only, dependency-only, or stale-path reports without a working repro and demonstrated OpenClaw impact.
    58	- Public internet exposure or risky deployment choices that the docs already recommend against.
    59	
    60	If you are unsure, report privately. We would rather route a careful report than miss a real boundary issue.
    61	
    62	### Duplicate Report Handling
    63	
    64	- Search existing advisories before filing.
    65	- Include likely duplicate GHSA IDs in your report when applicable.

    67	
    68	## Security Posture and Report Rules
    69	
    70	The sections below are the normative posture maintainers use for report triage. The headings are editorial; the policy text defines the boundary.
    71	
    72	### Detailed Report Acceptance Gate
    73	
    74	For fastest triage, include all of the following:
    75	
    76	- Exact vulnerable path (`file`, function, and line range) on a current revision.
    77	- Tested version details (OpenClaw version and/or commit SHA).
    78	- Reproducible PoC against latest `main` or latest released version.
    79	- If the claim targets a released version, evidence from the shipped tag and published artifact/package for that exact version (not only `main`).
    80	- For dependency CVE reports, evidence that the shipped dependency version is actually affected, plus a PoC that reproduces impact through OpenClaw. Showing that OpenClaw can reach a native parser is not enough by itself.
    81	- Demonstrated impact tied to OpenClaw's documented trust boundaries.
    82	- For exposed-secret reports: proof the credential is OpenClaw-owned (or grants access to OpenClaw-operated infrastructure/services).
    83	- Explicit statement that the report does not rely on adversarial operators sharing one gateway host/config.
    84	- Scope check explaining why the report is **not** covered by the Out of Scope section below.
    85	- For command-risk/parity reports (for example obfuscation detection differences), a concrete boundary-bypass path is required (auth/approval/allowlist/sandbox). Parity-only findings are treated as hardening, not vulnerabilities.

    87	Reports that miss these requirements may be closed as `invalid` or `no-action`.

    89	### Detailed False-Positive Patterns
    90	
    91	These are frequently reported but are typically closed with no code change:
    92	
    93	- Prompt-injection-only chains without a boundary bypass (prompt injection is out of scope).
    94	- Operator-intended local features (for example TUI local `!` shell) presented as remote injection.
    95	- Reports that treat explicit operator-control surfaces (for example browser evaluate/script execution or direct `node.invoke` execution primitives) as vulnerabilities without demonstrating an auth/policy/sandbox boundary bypass. These capabilities are intentional when enabled and are trusted-operator features, not standalone security bugs.
    96	- Reports that treat an admin-gated enablement or arming step as requiring `operator.admin` for every subsequent action, when the documented contract delegates use of the enabled capability to `operator.write` and no auth, arming, allowlist, sandbox, or policy bypass is shown. This is an arm-then-use operator guardrail, not privilege escalation.
    97	- Authorized user-triggered local actions presented as privilege escalation. Example: an allowlisted/owner sender running `/export-session /absolute/path.html` to write on the host. In this trust model, authorized user actions are trusted host actions unless you demonstrate an auth/sandbox/boundary bypass.
    98	- Reports that only show a malicious plugin executing privileged actions after a trusted operator installs/enables it.
    99	- Reports that assume per-user multi-tenant authorization on a shared gateway host/config.
   100	- Reports that only show quoted/replied/thread/forwarded supplemental context from non-allowlisted senders being visible to the model, without demonstrating an auth, policy, approval, or sandbox boundary bypass.
   101	- Reports that treat the Gateway HTTP compatibility endpoints (`POST /v1/chat/completions`, `POST /v1/responses`) as if they implemented scoped operator auth (`operator.write` vs `operator.admin`). These endpoints authenticate the shared Gateway bearer secret/password and are documented full operator-access surfaces, not per-user/per-scope boundaries.

For shared-secret auth (`gateway.auth.mode="token"` or `"password"`), those endpoints ignore narrower bearer-declared scopes and restore the full default operator scope set plus owner semantics.

     5	## Exposure posture and pre-flight

    45
